name: Cacio E Pepe (Spaghetti with Black Pepper and Pecorino Romano)
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt treats this three-ingredient Roman pasta as a deceptively hard dish, since the two classic failures - a thin greasy sauce or stubborn clumps of cheese - both come from trying to make something creamy out of a hard, dry, aged cheese. He explains that aged Pecorino is low in moisture and prone to breaking, which starchy pasta water fixes, while its tight protein structure tangles into lumps if heated too fast. His answers are to grate the cheese as finely as possible on a Microplane so it melts evenly, and to use two pans: one to boil the pasta and a second, cooler one in which the sauce is built. The second pan brought an unexpected bonus, since toasting the pepper in oil there mellows and sweetens it, and he cooks the spaghetti in just enough water to cover so the starch stays concentrated, lifting the pasta straight across with tongs instead of draining.
comment_digest: The most-endorsed point, echoing the article, is that the cheese must be ground truly fine - one reviewer with two votes says skipping that left a cheese ball the size of a tennis ball. A highly rated comment credits the method as written and reports no clumping. Alternatives appear for cooks who still struggle: one describes a Roman restaurant method of working powdered cheese and pepper into a paste with ice water so no heat touches the sauce until it meets the hot pasta; another returns drained pasta to the pot and stirs the cheese in thirds with the lid on two to three minutes between additions. Dissent exists - one cook who weighed everything and used a Microplane still got an oily result across four attempts, and another warns too much cheese always clumps and that hand-grating rock-hard Pecorino blows past the stated 20 minutes. Popular additions: minced garlic in the pepper oil, plus shrimp or chicken.
flags: Several comments end in 'Read More' and may be truncated.
